When you run a query in PostgreSQL, the database first creates a query plan — a detailed roadmap of how it will fetch the data (e.g., use an index, scan a table, perform a join, etc.).

🧠 The EXPLAIN command shows you that plan before actually running the query.

For example:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE city = 'Casablanca';
```

Without an index on city → Sequential Scan (checks all rows).

With an index on city → Index Scan (jumps directly to matching rows).

You could create the index like this:

CREATE INDEX idx_customers_city ON customers(city);


Then re-run:

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE city = 'Casablanca';

Mini-plan

Recall: EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows real timings.

Now: read join nodes: Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join — when each appears.

Quick mental model

Nested Loop: good when one side is small and you have an index to probe the big table.

Hash Join: good for large–large joins without a useful index; builds a hash of one side.

Merge Join: good when both inputs are sorted (or can use indexes to deliver sorted data).

Example query (Morocco context, English columns):

EXPLAIN SELECT *
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.city = 'Casablanca';


You might see one of:

Nested Loop -> Index Scan on orders (customer_id)

Hash Join -> Hash on customers

Merge Join -> Sort/Index paths on both

Seq Scan → it will read every row.

cost=0.00..1234.00 → planner’s guess of total work.

rows=500 → expected number of matching rows.

width=64 → average bytes per row.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE (planner + real execution)

PostgreSQL actually runs the query.

It shows both the estimated values and the real measured times.

Example:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM customers WHERE city = 'Casablanca';


Output:

Seq Scan on customers  (cost=0.00..1234.00 rows=500 width=64)
                      (actual time=0.04..8.23 rows=520 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.10 ms
Execution Time: 8.30 ms

When you run a query, PostgreSQL’s planner tries many possible ways to execute it — different join orders, index uses, scans, etc.
It picks the lowest-cost plan and shows it in EXPLAIN.

Let’s break the key pieces one by one.

🧩 1. Node Type (method)

This is how PostgreSQL will get the data.

Common types:

Node Type	What It Means
Seq Scan	Reads the whole table row by row.
Index Scan	Uses an index to jump directly to matching rows.
Bitmap Index Scan / Heap Scan	Uses index to mark blocks, then reads them in bulk (faster for many matches).
Nested Loop / Hash Join / Merge Join	Three main join algorithms.
Aggregate / Sort / Limit / Group / Filter	Extra operations applied after scanning or joining.
💰 2. Cost = startup..total

Example:

(cost=0.00..1234.00)


Startup cost = work before first row appears (e.g., sorting).

Total cost = estimated total work for all rows (includes startup).

Units are abstract — not time in ms! They’re used only to compare plans.

Postgres calculates cost from:

Disk page reads (cheaper if cached)

CPU operations

Row count estimates

The planner chooses the plan with the lowest total cost.

📊 3. rows

Example:

rows=500


This is the estimated number of output rows from that step.
It comes from:

Table statistics stored in pg_stats

The ANALYZE command (which refreshes stats)

Filters and selectivity estimates

If stats are old or wrong → the planner’s guess is bad → maybe a slow plan.

📦 4. width

Example:

width=64


Average bytes per row the planner expects (based on column data types and averages).
Used to estimate memory and I/O cost.

⚙️ 5. Extra details (indentation)

Indented lines show which node feeds into which:

Nested Loop
  -> Index Scan on orders ...
  -> Seq Scan on customers ...


Arrows mean “child node → parent node” (data flow upward).

🧩 6. With EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Adds actual:

actual time=start..end — measured milliseconds.

rows — real number of rows.

loops — how many times that node ran.

You can compare estimated vs actual rows to judge planner accuracy.

✅ Mini summary table

Part	Meaning
Node type	Execution method
cost=a..b	Planner’s estimated work
rows	Estimated row count
width	Estimated row size
actual time	Real timings (only with ANALYZE)

PostgreSQL doesn’t measure cost in milliseconds — it uses relative units so it can compare plans independently of hardware speed.

Each action (CPU step, disk read, etc.) has a weight:

Parameter	Meaning	Default
seq_page_cost	Cost to read one page (block) sequentially	1.0
random_page_cost	Cost to read one page randomly	4.0
cpu_tuple_cost	CPU cost per row processed	0.01
cpu_index_tuple_cost	CPU cost per index entry	0.005
cpu_operator_cost	CPU cost per comparison	0.0025

So if a plan’s total cost is, say, 100, that just means “≈100 units of work.”
Another plan with cost 80 is expected to be faster — even though neither number maps directly to milliseconds.

How nodes “feed” each other (the plan tree)

In an EXPLAIN output, indentation shows which node supplies rows to another.
Data flows upward in the plan — children produce rows that parents consume.

Example:

Nested Loop  (cost=0.43..50.00 rows=10 width=128)
  -> Index Scan using idx_customers_city on customers  (cost=0.43..20.00 rows=5 width=64)
        Index Cond: (city = 'Casablanca'::text)
  -> Index Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders  (cost=0.43..6.00 rows=2 width=64)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = customers.id)


🔹 The bottom nodes (Index Scans) are the sources — they read from tables.
🔹 The parent node (Nested Loop) takes their outputs and combines them (here, one order per customer).
🔹 The final result goes to the top of the tree (the client).

You can picture it like water pipes:

[orders index]    [customers index]
       ↘             ↙
         [Nested Loop join]
                ↓
           [Output rows]

           he leaf nodes are [orders index] and [customers index] — those are the ones that actually read data from the tables.

They’re called scan nodes because they scan a table or index to produce rows.
Everything above them (like Nested Loop, Hash Join, Aggregate, etc.) just processes those rows further.

Here’s the structure again with labels:

Nested Loop (parent)
  -> Index Scan on customers (leaf)
  -> Index Scan on orders (leaf)


➡️ Data flows upward:
Indexes → Tables → Join → Output.

Why use plain EXPLAIN when EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives real data?

It’s all about safety and speed.

Case	What happens	When to use
EXPLAIN	Just shows the plan — no query execution.	✅ Safe for slow or destructive queries (e.g., huge UPDATE, DELETE, or multi-hour SELECT).
EXPLAIN ANALYZE	Actually runs the query to measure time and row counts.	✅ Great for testing or tuning a query that’s safe and fast to run.

Imagine this query:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date < '2010-01-01';


That would really delete rows 😱 — not what you want just to see the plan.

So in production, we use:

EXPLAIN DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date < '2010-01-01';


to preview the cost and method without executing it.

⚡ Speed difference

EXPLAIN runs instantly (no data touched).

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the full query, which can take seconds, minutes, or hours depending on size.
